title: Security Advisory for Rust crates
description: Security Advisory for Rust crates on GitHub

items.content_html:
In rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45, application data that a client buffers before the handshake completes is sent to the server even when the server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).

When the server rejects ECH, the client completes the handshake with the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the ECH config's public_name. At the end of the handshake, start_traffic() encrypts and queues any plaintext buffered by ClientConnection::writer(). It does this before checking for EchStatus::Rejected and queueing the ech_required alert.

The application then receives Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello), as expected. However, the client is still expected to call write_tls() to send the fatal alert, and that call also sends the encrypted application data. The server decrypts the data and only then receives the alert.

The ordering bug is older than 0.23.44. Before 0.23.44, the client checked the server certificate against the inner server name rather than public_name, so a correctly configured server failed certificate verification first and no data was sent. 0.23.44 fixed that check, which makes the ordinary rejection path reachable.

Impact

Plaintext meant for the inner server, the one named in the encrypted ClientHello, goes to the client-facing server identified by public_name. That server is properly authenticated, so this is not an attack by an unauthenticated party. However this violates RFC 9849, which says the following:

  • Section 6.1.6: if the handshake and authentication succeed after ECH rejection, the client "MUST ... abort the connection with an "ech_required" alert before sending any application data to the server."
  • Section 6.1.7: the certificate is checked only against public_name, and the connection "MUST NOT" be reported as successful to the application. rustls does report failure correctly. The problem is only that data is sent before the alert.

This affects only clients that meet all of these conditions:

  • They use EchMode::Enable. GREASE ECH is not affected.
  • They write application data before the handshake completes.
  • They connect to a server that rejects their ECH config, for example because the config is stale. This is the same case where the server returns retry configs.

The usual client response to rejection is to retry with the server's retry configs. In that case, the data has already gone to the outer server.

References

  • https://github.com/rustls/rustls/security/advisories/GHSA-vp88-798v-h67f
  • https://github.com/rustls/rustls/pull/3300
  • https://github.com/rustls/rustls/pull/3354

items.content_html:
Summary

The client records the server-selected key-exchange group per server name when it processes the ServerHello, before the server is authenticated. A network attacker can answer one connection attempt for a target name with a ServerHello that selects X25519 and close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that name carry one X25519 share while supported_groups still lists X25519MLKEM768 first. If the server accepts that share instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only and no error.

An attacker that answers one connection attempt for the target name with a ServerHello selecting X25519 changes every later ClientHello of that client for that name, for as long as the entry stays in the store. No certificate or completed handshake is needed: it parses the ClientHello, sends the ServerHello, and closes.

TLS 1.3 transcript binding stops an on-path attacker from editing the ClientHello of one connection. It does not stop the attacker from steering the client's prediction state beforehand, because that state is written from an unauthenticated message.

What does not trigger it

  • Servers that send a HelloRetryRequest. The connection stays hybrid and costs one extra round trip.
  • A client configuration with resumption disabled: nothing is stored.
  • A different server name: the record is per name.

Impact

If the genuine server picks the group for which a share is present, instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only, between two peers that both support the hybrid group. No error is raised. The confidentiality of recorded sessions against a future quantum adversary is lost for those connections (harvest now, decrypt later). There is no key compromise and no authentication bypass.

Note that this behaviour is discussed at length in draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction so the actual security impact is largely down to a server policy decision.

References

  • https://github.com/rustls/rustls/security/advisories/GHSA-w44r-93j7-qv28
  • https://github.com/rustls/rustls/pull/3355
  • https://github.com/rustls/rustls/commit/8fa0dc5d517a63411ad1e528249bdf5b098ae5e4

items.content_html:
Summary

Formatting a client session value with Debug exposes its TLS 1.2 master secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK. A custom session store that logs these values can disclose keys to readers of the logs. Ordinary connection and built-in cache diagnostics remain redacted, and the session-store interface already warns that its values are sensitive.

Details

Derived formatters traverse the session's secret-bearing fields. This conflicts with the project's explicit key-material redaction policy.

Proof of concept

Custom ClientSessionStore implementations could leak secret data by using the provided Tls12ClientSessionValue or Tls13ClientSessionValue in a way that triggers its implementation of the Debug trait.

Impact

Such store implementations could leak the master secret for the TLS connection.

Acknowledgement

Thanks to OpenAI OutboundDisclosures@openai.com for the disclosure.

items.content_html:
Summary

The built-in (but disabled by default) Brotli certificate decoder bounds the output buffer but accepts an input-selected history window. A header of five bytes can specify a 1 GiB window allocation. A peer can abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request. A client must enable Brotli and connect to the peer; a server must enable Brotli and request a client certificate. Neither direction requires a trusted attacker certificate.

Details

rustls calls BrotliDecompress which enables Brotli's large-window extension. rustls applies a limit to certificates, but this applies to the decompressed result, and not to any internal allocations the process requires.

Impact

Client applications that enable the brotli feature will be vulnerable to malicious servers. Server applications that enable the brotli feature and enable client authentication will be vulnerable to malicious clients.

Potential for denial of service due to memory exhaustion from peers sending malicious Brotli-encoded certificates, for applications that enable Brotli decompression.

Acknowledgement

Thanks to OpenAI OutboundDisclosures@openai.com for the disclosure.

items.content_html:
Summary

Wasmtime may panic when the host lowers a component model stream or future into a guest, if the host created that stream or future with one payload type and the guest expects a different one. This can happen when an embedder creates a stream or future, passes it through a guest, receives it back under a type-erased type such as StreamAny or FutureAny, and then passes it to a guest function with a different payload type.

GHSA-63h4-6cx9-pjfj is a related advisory also fixing issues within this area, and this advisory is being issued for portions of Wasmtime that were not fixed as part of that advisory.

Impact

This affects embedders that do all of the following:

  1. Create streams or futures on the host with StreamReader::new or FutureReader::new
  2. Pass them to guest code and receive them back as StreamAny, FutureAny, Val::Stream/Val::Future, or a typed reader whose payload is one of these.
  3. Pass them on to a guest function whose stream or future payload type differs from the type the host created them with.

A guest can cause the mismatch in step 3 when it controls the types of the functions it exports or of the values it returns. In that case a malicious guest can make the host panic, a denial of service. Embedders that only use statically typed StreamReader<T>/FutureReader<T> with concrete payload types throughout, or that never pass streams or futures they created through a guest and back, are not affected.

items.content_html:
Summary

In Wasmtime prior to v43, the Cranelift compiler backend bit-packs its SSA value indices in a way that can result in silent overflow in release builds, and result in incorrect value references in the IR resulting in arbitrary miscompilation. A very large Wasm function body, or one that is specially crafted to use many SSA values, can use this to force type-confusion or other arbitrary side-effects and escape the sandbox.

Cranelift was changed in Wasmtime v43 to use a full u32 index, with checks if that limit is exceeded, and so is no longer susceptible to this bug.

Impact

A Wasmtime engine with default settings (using the Cranelift backend) on any architecture/platform could experience a sandbox escape from a specially-crafted Wasm module.

Patches

Wasmtime v36.0.19 has been released which fixes this issue.

References

  • https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-897f-g5gm-fmxm

items.content_html:
Impact

Fallow expands some globs from the analyzed repository on disk. Before 3.34.0, a segment such as .*, .? or ..* in such a glob also matched the special .. entry. The glob crate tests .. against a segment that starts with a literal .. Fallow validates plugin glob patterns and refuses absolute paths and .. segments, but these segments passed that validation.

The attacker controls the repository content. The attacker must also be able to read the Fallow output, for example a CI log or a pull request comment. Then the attacker can learn if a file or directory exists in the parent of the project root:

  • A plugin fileExists detection pattern such as .*/marker.json made the plugin active when marker.json existed in the parent directory.
  • An external plugin configPatterns or alwaysUsed pattern could match a config file in the parent directory. When the plugin was active and declared toolingDependencies, the tooling detection credited the related dev dependency. An unused dependency finding could then disappear, and --trace-dependency printed the outside path.
  • fallow plugin-check reported path_exists: true for a seeded entry that matched only in the parent directory.

Fallow tested only that these paths exist. It did not read or print the content of a file outside the project root through these globs.

The Jest, Vitest and Rstest project globs had the same .* problem, and the Jest and Vitest ones also read file content. GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5 describes that case.

Patches

Fixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now rewrites a leading . in a wildcard segment to [.] before it expands the glob on disk. [.] matches the same hidden files and directories inside the project root. The glob crate does not test .. against it.

Workarounds

Run Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the detection, configPatterns and alwaysUsed patterns of its plugin files.

items.content_html:
Impact

items.title: [fallow-cli] Fallow: A `.*` glob segment let an analyzed repository make Fallow test paths in the parent of the project root

items.content_html:
Impact

Fallow reads the Jest and Vitest configs of the repository that it analyzes. A Jest projects entry or a Vitest test.projects entry can name a path. Fallow followed such an entry to a config file and read that file, also when the file was outside the project root. These forms reached outside the root:

  • an absolute path or glob, for example /etc/*;
  • a path with .. segments, for example ../*;
  • a glob with a .* segment, because the glob crate also tests .. against a segment that starts with a literal .;
  • a symlink in the project root to a directory above it;
  • the extends path of a Vitest inline project;
  • a script --config path that is a symlink to a file outside the project root.

Fallow parsed each of these files as a test runner config. Fallow used the content only to credit dependencies, setup files and JSX import sources. Thus unused dependency and unused file findings could change. Fallow did not print the content or send it over the network.

The Fallow threat model states that analysis reads only inside the project root. A crafted repository could make Fallow read files that the user did not expect. Such a read can happen in CI, or when an agent runs Fallow on a cloned repository. The attacker gets changed findings, not the file content.

Versions 2.68.0 to 3.33.1 read outside files through Jest projects. Version 3.33.1 also read them through Vitest test.projects.

Patches

Fixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now resolves each match with symlinks and .. segments removed. Fallow reads the match only when it is inside the project root. A glob whose literal base is outside the project root does not run. The boundary is the project root, so an in-root entry such as <rootDir>/../packages/* still works, also from the config of a workspace package. Fallow also does not read a script --config path that is a symlink to a file outside the project root.

Workarounds

Run Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the projects entries of its jest.config.* and vitest.config.* files.

items.content_html:
Summary

On the multi-threaded runtime, there is a race condition between Interval::poll_tick and the runtime's time driver.

This affects Interval only. Sleep and Timeout are not affected.

Details

In Tokio v1.54.0, a race condition between tokio::time::Interval::poll_tick (including .tick().await) and the runtime time driver can drop an internal timer entry without synchronizing with the driver thread that is firing it. This causes a data race and use-after-free on the timer's waker and task state in safe Rust, leading to assertion panics, task reference-count corruption, or heap memory corruption.

This bug was introduced by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8458, and it was fixed by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8692.

Impact

This may lead to crashes and use-after-frees in applications using Interval on a multi-threaded runtime.

Since this issue is known to lead to crashes in production systems, the v1.54.0 release of Tokio has been yanked.

Credits

Thank you to creepycode and carabistouille for reporting this privately using the procedure outlined in our security policy. They both reported the issue independently of each other.

items.content_html:
Summary

In the gix crate, Cache::protect_options() in gix/src/config/cache/access.rs reads the three filesystem path-protection settings (core.protectHFS, core.protectNTFS, and gitoxide.core.protectWindows) with the unfiltered gix_config::File::boolean() accessor instead of the trust-aware boolean_filter() accessor used by every other security-critical config read in the same file. When a repository is opened with reduced trust (an ownership mismatch, which maps .git/config sections to Trust::Reduced), these protection settings should not be honored from the untrusted repository-local config. Because the trust filter is skipped, an attacker who controls a repository's .git/config on a shared filesystem can set core.protectNTFS = false and/or core.protectHFS = false, disabling the .git path-confusion checks that run during checkout, index creation, merge, and tree editing. On case-insensitive filesystems this lets crafted tree entries resolve to the .git directory and overwrite hooks or config.

Root Cause

Repositories opened under Trust::Reduced install a section filter (is_trusted) so that security-relevant settings coming from an untrusted repository-local .git/config are ignored. The Cache struct stores this filter and applies it throughout gix/src/config/cache/access.rs for diff drivers, merge drivers, URL rewrites, scheme permissions, lock timeout, and checkout workers. protect_options() is the exception: it reads the path-protection booleans through self.resolved.boolean(...), which delegates to boolean_filter(key, |_| true) and therefore accepts values from every section regardless of trust. As a result, an untrusted repository-local setting of core.protectHFS/core.protectNTFS/gitoxide.core.protectWindows overrides the safe defaults, defeating the trust boundary for exactly the controls that are meant to prevent .git path-confusion attacks.

gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:300  Cache::protect_options() : vulnerable function
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:306  self.resolved.boolean(gitoxide.core.protectWindows)  (unfiltered)
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:310  self.resolved.boolean(core.protectHFS)              (unfiltered)
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:314  self.resolved.boolean(core.protectNTFS)             (unfiltered)
gix-config/src/file/access/comfort.rs:89  boolean() delegates to boolean_filter(key, |_| true)
gix/src/config/mod.rs:61  is_trusted() : the filter that would reject untrusted repo-local sections
gix-validate/src/path.rs:98  component() : path validation that honors the resulting options

Impact

An attacker who owns a repository on a filesystem shared with the victim (a multi-user development host, a shared or network-mounted checkout, or a CI workspace reused across jobs) edits that repository's .git/config to disable one or both of core.protectHFS and core.protectNTFS. When the victim opens the repository with a gix-based tool, the ownership mismatch yields Trust::Reduced, which should neutralize these untrusted settings, but protect_options() honors them anyway. The attacker also commits tree entries whose names are filesystem-specific encodings of .git (for example NTFS short names such as GIT~1, NTFS alternate-data-stream or trailing-dot/space variants, or HFS+ forms using ignorable code points). When the victim performs a checkout, index build, merge, or tree edit, path validation no longer rejects these names, so on a case-insensitive filesystem (Windows NTFS, macOS HFS+) they collapse to the real .git directory. This permits overwriting repository hooks and configuration, which plausibly leads to arbitrary command execution in the victim's context on the next Git operation that runs a hook. The confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact follows from control over the victim's .git directory and any resulting hook execution; hook execution was not freshly executed here and is characterized as the plausible consequence of the demonstrated path-protection bypass.

Proof of Concept

The following unit test places the config cache in the exact state produced after a submodule or repository is initialized (only url copied to the local config) and shows that the attacker's path-protection override from the repository-local config is honored even though it should be filtered under reduced trust. The same boolean() vs boolean_filter() discrepancy is directly observable in source.

// Demonstrates that core.protectNTFS from an untrusted repository-local
// section is honored by the unfiltered read in protect_options().
use std::str::FromStr;

// Trusted (system/global) config: protection on by default.
// Untrusted repository-local config (.git/config) disables NTFS protection.
let repo_local = gix_config::File::from_str("[core]\n    protectNTFS = false").unwrap();

// Reading core.protectNTFS with the trust-aware filter would reject the
// repository-local section; reading it unfiltered (as protect_options does)
// returns Some(false), disabling the .git-confusion check.
let filtered = repo_local.boolean_filter("core.protectNTFS", |_| false); // trusted-only
let unfiltered = repo_local.boolean("core.protectNTFS");                  // what protect_options uses
eprintln!("filtered (trusted only) = {:?}", filtered);   // None  -> safe default kept
eprintln!("unfiltered (vulnerable) = {:?}", unfiltered); // Some(Ok(false)) -> protection disabled

filtered (trusted only) = None
unfiltered (vulnerable) = Some(Ok(false))

Source confirmation that boolean() performs no trust filtering:

// gix-config/src/file/access/comfort.rs:89
pub fn boolean(&self, key: impl AsKey) -> Result<Option<bool>> {
    self.boolean_filter(key, |_| true)
}

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: The attacker owns a repository on a filesystem shared with the victim; the victim opens it with a gix-based tool, and the ownership mismatch sets the repository's config sections to Trust::Reduced (gix/src/open/options.rs:215 installs the is_trusted section filter).
  2. Control: The attacker writes core.protectNTFS = false (and/or core.protectHFS = false) into the repository-local .git/config, plus tree entries whose names are filesystem-specific encodings of .git.
  3. Path: During checkout, index build, merge, or tree edit, each call site invokes protect_options() (gix/src/clone/checkout.rs:103, gix/src/repository/index.rs:206, gix/src/repository/merge.rs:153 and :214, gix/src/object/tree/editor.rs:24, gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:362).
  4. Guard: The is_trusted filter (gix/src/config/mod.rs:61) would reject the untrusted repository-local section, but protect_options() reads via self.resolved.boolean(...) (gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:306,310,314), which delegates to boolean_filter(key, |_| true) and ignores the filter.
  5. Primitive: gix_validate::path::component() (gix-validate/src/path.rs:98) receives protect_hfs=false and/or protect_ntfs=false, so the HFS+/NTFS .git-confusion checks are skipped. When only one protection is disabled, the combined-case fallback at gix-validate/src/path.rs:137 does not run, and the remaining single-filesystem check does not cover the other filesystem's encodings.
  6. Result: Crafted tree entries that encode .git pass validation and are written to disk; on a case-insensitive filesystem they resolve into the real .git directory, overwriting hooks and configuration and plausibly yielding code execution in the victim's context.

Bypass Evidence

The protection under test is the reduced-trust section filter that is supposed to stop untrusted repository-local config from altering security settings. The strongest counter-argument is the case-insensitive .git fallback in gix-validate/src/path.rs:137, which rejects a plain .git match when both HFS+ and NTFS protections are off. That fallback is insufficient for two reasons verified in source: it only runs when BOTH protect_hfs and protect_ntfs are false (!(protect_hfs | protect_ntfs) at line 137), so disabling a single protection leaves it inactive; and even when it runs, its exact eq_ignore_ascii_case(b".git") test does not cover filesystem-specific encodings such as NTFS short names (GIT~1), NTFS trailing-dot/space or alternate-data-stream forms, or HFS+ ignorable-code-point variants, which are precisely what the dedicated is_dot_hfs/is_dot_git_ntfs checks (now skipped) exist to catch. The boolean() accessor was confirmed to apply no trust filtering (gix-config/src/file/access/comfort.rs:89), and the sibling reads in the same file consistently apply filter_config_section, so the unfiltered read is a genuine deviation rather than an intentional exemption. This issue is distinct from the previously disclosed submodule command-execution bypass (CVE-2026-40034 / GHSA-f26g-jm89-4g65): that advisory's fix changed only the gix-submodule crate and gix/src/repository/submodule.rs and never touched protect_options(), so this code path and its remediation boundary are not covered by it.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: rust
  • Package: gix (crates.io)
  • Confirmed affected range: >= 0.88.0, <= 0.89.0
  • Latest release checked: 0.89.0 (crates.io)
  • Fix status: 0.90.0

protect_options() was introduced in gix 0.88.0 and did not exist in earlier releases; before then the path-validation options were not configurable from repository config in this way. The unfiltered read is present from introduction through the latest published release (0.89.0).

Suggested Fix

Read the path-protection settings through the same trust-aware accessor used by the other security-critical reads in gix/src/config/cache/access.rs: replace each self.resolved.boolean(...) call in protect_options() with self.resolved.boolean_filter(..., &mut self.filter_config_section.clone()) so that untrusted repository-local sections are excluded under Trust::Reduced and the safe defaults are retained. The fix must apply to all three keys (core.protectHFS, core.protectNTFS, gitoxide.core.protectWindows) so that no single protection can be disabled from untrusted config. As an interim mitigation, operators can avoid opening untrusted or other-user-owned repositories with gix-based tools on shared or case-insensitive filesystems; this does not remove the underlying bypass.

Reported by zx.

References

items.content_html:
Librsvg uses libxml2, a C library, to parse XML. When librsvg parses an SVG document which has a nested Xinclude, an XML entity declaration with a duplicate name as an existing one can cause a use-after-free error.

While libxml2 is expanding an internal entity, a recursive XInclude can parse another document that declares an entity with the same name. Both parses use the same XmlState entity map on the librsvg side. entity_insert() replaces the first entry, whose Drop implementation calls xmlFreeNode(). The outer xmlCtxtParseEntity() then keeps using the freed 144-byte xmlEntity.

The included parse should not free an entity that the outer parser is still using.

The fix is in commit 8a1b0cd319e9af2d1e9cf878081dd77f227a0504, where librsvg will no longer free xmlEntity pointers that libxml2 is still using.
